opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important questions in robot learning right now. The way I think about it, there's a spectrum of data sources, and they each contribute something different.

At one end you have things like internet video and language data. That's incredibly abundant, and it can teach a model a lot about the world: what objects are, how people tend to interact with them, what the goal of a task might look like. But it doesn't tell you much about the low-level details of how to actually move a robot's body. There's an embodiment gap.

At the other end you have real robot data: teleoperated demonstrations, or the robot's own autonomous experience. That's much more expensive to collect, but it's the data that actually captures the physics, the contact, and the fine-grained motor control. In my experience, there really isn't a substitute for having a good amount of real robot data, especially for dexterous tasks where things like friction and deformable objects matter a lot.

One thing I've come to appreciate is that diversity matters more than sheer volume. If you collect a huge amount of data in one lab, on one table, with the same objects and lighting, you get a policy that's pretty brittle. Collecting data across many environments, many objects, and many different robots tends to generalize much better, even if the total amount is smaller. We've seen that pretty consistently: training on data from many robot platforms can actually help performance on any individual platform.

The other piece I'm really excited about is the robot's own experience: letting it practice, make mistakes, and recover. Demonstrations usually show the happy path, but a lot of what makes a policy robust is knowing what to do when things go slightly wrong. So I think the recipe is something like: pretrain on broad data to get general knowledge, use diverse real-world robot data to ground that in physical skills, and then let the robot improve on its own experience, potentially with some human feedback, to get the reliability you need for real deployment.

r002.rationale: It values robots learning from their own practice and mistakes, but does not connect this to language models bootstrapping through reinforcement learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about it as a few different buckets, and they each play a different role.

The first is data that's collected directly on the robot, usually through teleoperation, where a person is actually guiding the robot through a task. That data is incredibly valuable because it's exactly the distribution you want the policy to learn from. It's the right embodiment, the right sensors, the right action space. The downside is that it's expensive. You need people, you need hardware, and you need time. So the question becomes how far you can get with that alone, and the answer is you can get surprisingly far, but you hit a ceiling in terms of coverage. The world has a long tail of objects and situations, and you can't teleoperate your way through all of it.

The second bucket is data from other robots and other embodiments. There's been a lot of work, including the Open X-Embodiment effort, showing that you can pool data across very different robots and actually get positive transfer. The arm looks different, the gripper is different, the cameras are mounted differently, and yet the model learns something general about how to move in the world and manipulate things. That was not obvious a few years ago. I would have guessed the transfer would be weak, and it turns out it's meaningful.

The third bucket is data that isn't robot data at all. Internet-scale video, language, images. This is where the vision-language-action models come in. You take a model that already understands what a mug is, what "put the spoon in the drawer" means, what a kitchen looks like, and then you teach it to act. The robot data is relatively small, but it's sitting on top of this huge foundation of semantic and visual knowledge. That's what gives you generalization to objects and instructions the robot has never seen during its own collection.

And then there's a fourth bucket that I think is going to matter a lot more over time, which is experience the robot generates on its own. Autonomous data collection, where the robot is out there trying things, sometimes with a person intervening, and you're learning from that. The nice thing is that this scales without the per-sample human cost of teleop, and the data naturally reflects the robot's own mistakes, which is exactly what you need to improve. The hard part is that you need the robot to be good enough to do something useful before that flywheel starts turning, and you need to be careful about what signal you're learning from.

So if I zoom out, the way I think about it is less "which kind of experience" and more "what's the right mix at each stage." Early on, pretraining on broad data, including non-robot data, gets you the priors. Teleop gets you the first competent policies. Cross-embodiment data broadens the coverage. And then on-robot autonomous experience is what lets you keep improving at scale without a human in the loop for every trajectory. I think the groups that figure out how to combine those well, rather than betting on any one of them, are the ones that will get to really capable robots.

r002.rationale: The response discusses autonomous robot data collection, but does not connect it to language models bootstrapping from their own experience through reinforcement learning.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that robots need experience interacting with the world. There’s a lot you can learn from watching videos—what objects look like, how people use them, what a successful task might look like. But that doesn’t necessarily tell you what will happen when you apply a particular force or move your gripper a little bit to the left. For that, having actions paired with their consequences is really valuable.

And I think diversity matters a lot. If you collect a huge amount of experience in one kitchen, with the same objects and the same lighting, you can get very good at that kitchen without learning something that transfers to someone else’s home. So we want experience across environments, objects, and tasks.

The other piece is experience recovering from mistakes. Human demonstrations can give you a good starting point, but the robot will inevitably get into situations the demonstrator never encountered. It needs to learn what to do when a grasp slips or an object ends up somewhere unexpected. That’s where letting robots try things, observe the outcome, and improve from that experience becomes really important.

r002.rationale: It supports robots trying actions and learning from outcomes, but does not connect autonomous experience to language models bootstrapping through reinforcement learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is getting experience that captures how your actions affect the world. A lot of the data we have today—images, text, even video—tells you something about what the world looks like and how it changes. But for a robot, you also need to understand: if I push this object, what happens? If I try to grasp it this way and it slips, how should I adjust?

So I expect we’ll need a combination of sources. Human video can provide a lot of breadth, demonstrations on robots can show how to accomplish tasks with a particular body, and then robots collecting their own experience can help fill in the gaps. That last part is particularly important because demonstrations tend to show successful behavior. A robot also needs experience making mistakes and recovering from them.

And I think diversity matters a lot. You don’t want a robot that can only pick up one object in one kitchen. You want experience across objects, environments, and tasks that lets it learn something transferable, so that when it encounters a new situation, it doesn’t have to start from scratch.
